2.text: Two women hold the ends of a line, and swing it around regularly, while a

3.text: third jumps over the middle of it, keeping her knees and heels together. I

4.text: have not noticed any particular rules about the order of the jumps, like those

5.text: found by Parry among the Iglulik Eskimo.¹
5.note: Footnote marker after "Eskimo." is the superscript digit ¹ (U+00B9), confirmed at 4x; mz/ocr rendered it as a plain "!". Per keying_spec.md §2.10 markers are always the superscript sort.

6.text: Another game is a contest in crawling on the knees, which is rather

7.text: difficult for women, on account of their clumsy breeches. In one sort of race

8.text: the contestants move around while bending forward and taking hold of the

9.text: toes of their boots with their hands. In another they crouch on the ground,

10.text: imitating the motion of the seal.

11.text: SONGS AND DANCES. — The dances performed at ceremonials by men or

12.text: women will be described farther on. Young girls have dances of their own,

13.text: which are meant to imitate the motions of various animals or certain human

14.text: actions. They are accompanied by peculiar songs, or rather rhythmical guttural

15.text: sounds produced by alternately drawing in and letting out the breath. The

16.text: act of making these sounds is termed “to call with the throat” (pič-eiñeˊrkɪn).
16.resolved: č = c + U+030C; ñ = n + U+0303; ˊ = U+02CA stress mark, on e before rk; ɪ = U+026A (dotless, in rkɪn — mz/ocr read this as "rkmn")

17.text: Two or more girls take positions opposite each other or in a circle (see Plate XXVII,

18.text: Fig. 4) and in succession produce the sounds, keeping time carefully, and

19.text: quickly taking their turns one after the other. The singing is begun with low

20.text: hoarse notes. Imitative sounds are introduced later in a much higher key.

21.text: While singing, the girls sway the upper part of their bodies back and forth,

22.text: and then go through various imitative motions in connection with the sounds

23.text: uttered (Plates XXXI, Fig. 2; XXVII, Fig. 4). Young boys taking part in the

24.text: dance hold up their hands and snap their fingers, at the same time producing

25.text: a peculiar clicking sound with their tongues. Each song, with the accompanying

26.text: dance, has the name of the animal represented.

27.text: The most frequently performed are the Raven and The-One-eyed-One

28.text: dances. The imitative sounds of the former represent the croaking of the

29.text: Raven. The girls for a while also keep repeating, “Raven, Raven !” in hoarse
29.note: Printed with a space before the exclamation mark (“Raven, Raven !”), confirmed at 4x. keying_spec.md §2.9 normalizes spacing only before ;/:/, — it does not name "!" — so this interword space is kept as printed rather than stripped.

31.text: around, pretend to seek for something, peck at the ground, etc. The song

32.text: of The-One-eyed-One is accompanied by a few words sung in the same manner

33.text: as “Raven.” It runs like this: “The-One-eyed-One called with his throat

36.text: The-One-eyed-One. He is supposed to have been an old man who wanted to

37.text: have a contest of “calling with the throat” with some young girls. In the

38.text: contest his only eye came out of the socket under the strain.

39.text: Among other songs may be mentioned “The Song of the Fox.” It is

40.text: a kind of dialogue between the fox and the bear, and reproduces a widely

41.text: known tale, in which the fox pretends to heal the bear’s wounds with red-hot

42.text: stones, and finally kills him. The fox speaks in a thin treble voice; the bear
